per_query.query: What is the mode of action and IRAC resistance group of abamectin?
per_query.answer: Abamectin acts as a glutamate‑gated chloride channel (GluCl) allozyme modulator that affects insect nerve and muscle action, causing paralysis [D1]. Its IRAC resistance classification is Group 6 (Avermectins) [D1].

evidence.label: D1
evidence.name: abamectin
evidence.content:
Active Substance: abamectin

Introduction: Mixture of abamectin B1a (major component) and B1b (minor component). Widely used macrolide insecticide and acaricide in large quantities.

Mode of action: Glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluCl) allozyme modulator that affects insect nerve and muscle action. Activation of glutamate-gated chloride channels after aliasing causes paralysis. Glutamate is an important inhibitory neurotransmitter in insects.

The way of action: Poor poisoning by touch, stomach, and internal absorption

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 6; Avermectins.

evidence.label: D2
evidence.name: azadirachtin
evidence.content:
Active Substance: azadirachtin

Resistance: IRAC UN Group; compounds with unknown or undetermined mechanism of action Neem (Azadirachtin)

evidence.label: D3
evidence.name: chlorpyrifos
evidence.content:
Active Substance: chlorpyrifos

Introduction: The common name for the analog dimethyl ester is chlorpyrifos-methyl.

Mode of action: Inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase (AChE; EC 3.1.1.7). Acts on the nervous system of pests. The enzyme terminates the action of the excitatory neurotransmitter acetylcholine at the synapse. The inhibition of its activity leads to increased levels of acetylcholine accumulation and constant activation of receptors in the postsynaptic membrane, causing hyperexcitability, spasms, paralysis and death of the pest.

The way of action: Touch, stomach and fumigation

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 1; 1B, Organophosphates.

evidence.label: D4
evidence.name: ametoctradin
evidence.content:
Active Substance: ametoctradin

Mode of action: Acts on complex III: cytochrome bc1 (ubiquinone reductase) at the Qo site, labeled pepstatin-binding subsite (FRAC 2022)

Resistance: Fungicide Resistance Action Committee International FRAC 45, C8, QoSI-Fungicide Group (Quinone Outside Inhibitor, stigmatellin binding type). There was no cross-resistance with the Quinone Outside Inhibitor QoI fungicide. Resistance risk is considered moderate to high (Unit Point Inhibitor) and requires resistance management.

evidence.label: D5
evidence.name: pirimicarb
evidence.content:
Active Substance: pirimicarb

Introduction: In France, the common name is spelled "pyrimicarbe". Aphicide with a positive temperature coefficient of carbamate. It is fast-acting and has a short residual period.

Mode of action: Inhibitor of acetolactate synthase (ALS; EC 2.2.1.6). Acts on the nervous system of pests. The enzyme terminates the action of the excitatory neurotransmitter acetylcholine at the synapse. Inhibition of its activity leads to increased levels of acetylcholine accumulation and constant activation of receptors in the postsynaptic membrane, causing hyperexcitability, spasms, paralysis and death of the pest.

The way of action: Touch, fumigation and penetration

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 1; 1A, carbamates (Carbamates).

per_query.query: How does fipronil affect GABA-gated chloride channels?
per_query.answer: Fipronil acts as a blocker of GABA‑gated chloride channels; it blocks GABA‑activated chloride channels, leading to hyperexcitability and convulsions in insects [D1].

evidence.label: D1
evidence.name: fipronil
evidence.content:
Active Substance: fipronil

Introduction: A racemate. The chemical structure is characterized by a central pyrazole ring with a phenyl group attached to one of the nitrogen atoms of the pyrazole. When the phenyl group is attached to one of the carbon atoms of the pyrazole ring, many of the molecules have excellent herbicidal activity.

Mode of action: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) gated chloride channel blocker that acts on the insect nervous system. It blocks GABA-activated chloride channels, thereby causing hyperexcitability and convulsions in insects.GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in neural excitatory transmission in insects.

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 2; 2B, Phenylpyrazoles (Phenylpyrazoles).

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 6; Avermectins.

evidence.name: bifenthrin
evidence.content:
Active Substance: bifenthrin

Introduction: A racemate. (1R,3R)-bifenthrin, or κ-bifenthrin, the international common name for the left-handed single enantiomer is kappa-bifenthrin.

Mode of action: Sodium channel modulator that acts on the insect nervous system. It keeps sodium channels open and causes hyperexcitability in insects. In some cases, it also causes a block in nerve conduction. Sodium channels are involved in the conduction of action potentials along nerve axons.

The way of action: Touch and stomach poison

per_query.query: What EPSPS-related mode of action is listed for glyphosate?
per_query.answer: The mode of action listed for glyphosate is “Inhibitor of 5‑enolpyruvyl mangiferyl‑3‑phosphate synthase (EPSPS)” [D1].

evidence.label: D1
evidence.name: glyphosate
evidence.content:
Active Substance: glyphosate

Introduction: Glyphosate is registered in more than 130 countries and is one of the most produced, used and sold herbicides in the world. Described by some as an "almost ideal" herbicide and a once-in-a-century discovery, glyphosate is as important to reliable global food production as penicillin is to the treatment of human disease. However, in March 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), a division of the World Health Organization, classified glyphosate as "probably carcinogenic to humans" (Group 2A) based on the results of epidemiological, animal and in vitro studies. Sites of carcinogenicity in humans: limited evidence for leukemia and/or lymphoma. Show more (Introduction to Glyphosate)

Mode of action: Inhibitor of 5-enolpyruvyl mangiferyl-3-phosphate synthase (EPSPS).

The way of action: Inactivation, endocytosis conduction

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 9. Glyphosate-resistant weeds had not yet been identified when the first genetically modified crops such as corn, oilseed rape, soybeans, and cotton were introduced in the 1990s. By 2014, glyphosate-resistant weeds dominated herbicide resistance research, with 23 resistant weeds, often referred to as "superweeds," identified in 18 countries. The most common resistant weeds are oxalis, matang, multiflora ryegrass, hard ryegrass, small whitebrier, balsam fescue, ragweed, groundsel, morningglory, tumbleweed, orang-utan, false sorghum, firleaf algae, fleabane and Palmer amaranth.

evidence.name: phenmedipham
evidence.content:
Active Substance: phenmedipham

Introduction: The generic name for the ethyl analog is "phenmedipham-ethyl".

Mode of action: Inhibition of photosynthesis photosystem II - Serine 264 binders (photosynthesis PS Ⅱ - Serine 264 binders)

The way of action: selectiveness

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 5

evidence.label: D3
evidence.name: glufosinate-ammonium
evidence.content:
Active Substance: glufosinate-ammonium

Introduction: A racemate. Touch type (with a certain degree of systemic) inactivating organophosphorus herbicide. After application, the ammonium metabolism in the weed body is put into disorder in a short time, and the cytotoxic agent ammonium ion accumulates in the plant body, resulting in serious inhibition of photosynthesis. It is a broad-spectrum, post-emergence herbicide, widely used in orchards, vineyards, non-cultivated land to prevent and eliminate annual and perennial dicotyledonous and grass weeds.

Mode of action: Inhibition of glutamine synthetase (GS; EC 6.3.1.2)

The way of action: annihilation (of soul, Sanskrit ?ā?vata-vāda)

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 10

evidence.label: D4
evidence.name: paraquat
evidence.content:
Active Substance: paraquat

Introduction: Paraquat is defined in ISO 1750-1981 as 1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridinium, while the anion contained is required to be indicated in commercial formulations. There are 2 face-to-face commercial salts, paraquat dichloride and paraquat bisulfate methyl ester, with its dichloride being widely used. Regardless of the salt, the active ingredient content is indicated by paraquat. Paraquat and paraquat dichloride are two compounds. Queries revealed that its toxicity and treatment accounted for the vast majority of the literature, indicating a great threat to the safety of human life. Despite all the efforts of pesticide producers (development of solid dosage forms; addition of the emetic triazolopyrimidinone to aqueous dosage forms, blue or green coloring agents, odorants and thickeners), they have not escaped the fate of being banned.

Mode of action: Photosystem I electron transport inhibitor

The way of action: Extinguishability, touch kills

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 22. Resistant weeds have emerged in Western Australia. Alternating or rotating with glyphosate may delay the development of weed resistance.

evidence.label: D5
evidence.name: diquat dibromide
evidence.content:
Active Substance: diquat dibromide

Introduction: The product when dibromoethane is used in the second cyclization step of the synthesis of diquat. Bromine or chloride ions can be readily identified by ion chromatography with anion column separation and conductivity detection. Diquat dibromide is a strong irritant and can somewhat dissuade suicidal people from taking it orally. Due to the placement of a bromine atom in the bipyridine system, it has a certain degree of internal absorption, but will not hurt the root system. Bipyridine herbicide, which is the world's third largest inoculative herbicide after glyphosate and paraquat, can be rapidly absorbed by the green tissue of plants, and quickly passivated after contact with the soil. It is mainly used in plots where broadleaf weeds are predominant, and is effective against malignant broadleaf weeds, with fast effect, strong conductivity and low-temperature resistance, and it can also be used for blighting and drying of rice and potato before harvesting.

Mode of action: Inhibitor of photosynthetic electron transport. Peroxides produced during photosynthesis that damage cell membranes and cytoplasm.

The way of action: Extinguishability, touch kills

Introduction: Hydrogen peroxide is a strong oxidizing agent that is easily explosive. It is usually commercially available as an aqueous solution and is subject to different regulations depending on its concentration. The main commercial products are aqueous solutions containing 30, 50, 70 or 90 per cent hydrogen peroxide and stabilizers to inhibit its decomposition. It combines with a number of compounds to form crystals that can be used as mild oxidizing agents, the best known of which is sodium perborate (NaBO2-H2O2-3H2O or NaBO3-4H2O). It reacts with certain organic compounds to form hydroperoxides or peroxides, several of which can be used to trigger polymerization reactions. Although it can be oxidized by a few compounds such as potassium permanganate, in most reactions it oxidizes other substances.

per_query.query: Which active substances affect chitin synthase 1 and disrupt normal arthropod growth or development?
per_query.answer:
Lufenuron is an inhibitor of chitin biosynthesis that affects chitin synthase 1 and interferes with normal insect growth and development [D1].  
Etoxazole is a mite growth inhibitor that affects chitin synthase 1 and interferes with normal mite growth and development [D2].  
Novaluron is an inhibitor of chitin biosynthesis that affects chitin synthase 1 and interferes with normal insect growth and development [D3].

evidence.name: lufenuron
evidence.content:
Active Substance: lufenuron

Introduction: A racemate.

Mode of action: Inhibitor of chitin biosynthesis affecting chitin synthase 1. Inhibits the enzyme that catalyzes the polymerization of chitin and interferes with normal insect growth and development.

The way of action: Keeps pests from molting or pupating properly.

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 15; benzoylureas.

evidence.content:

Introduction: Specific triazine insect growth regulator against American spotted fly. It has a strong endocannabinoid conductive effect, and has a strong inhibitory effect on the development of egg larvae of Diptera insects (such as subterranean flies, gall midge, gophers, root maggots) and larvae of some Coleoptera insects. It can make the larvae deformed morphologically and unable to pupate normally.

Mode of action: Inhibits the activity of chitin synthase.

The way of action: Keeps pests from molting or pupating properly.

Active Substance: imazethapyr

Introduction: A racemate. Systemic conductive selective soybean field herbicide. For use in preemergence soil or early postemergence stem and leaf spray treatments to control amaranth, polygonum, quinoa, lobelia, abutilon, alewife, barnyard grass, dogwood, matang, and millet in spring soybean fields. It is harmless to soybean and other leguminous crops at the recommended dose.

Mode of action: Acetolactate synthase (ALS; EC 2.2.1.6), also known as acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS; EC 2.2.1.6) inhibitor. Inhibits the biosynthesis of the branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine, disrupting protein synthesis and thereby interfering with DNA synthesis and cell division and growth, ultimately leading to plant death. Soybean and peanut selectively derive rapid detoxification from demethylation and glycosylation.

The way of action: selectiveness

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 2

evidence.label: D2
evidence.name: abamectin
evidence.content:
Active Substance: abamectin

Introduction: Mixture of abamectin B1a (major component) and B1b (minor component). Widely used macrolide insecticide and acaricide in large quantities.

Mode of action: Glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluCl) allozyme modulator that affects insect nerve and muscle action. Activation of glutamate-gated chloride channels after aliasing causes paralysis. Glutamate is an important inhibitory neurotransmitter in insects.

The way of action: Poor poisoning by touch, stomach, and internal absorption

Resistance: International Insecticide Resistance Action Committee IRAC Group 6; Avermectins.

evidence.name: thiram
evidence.content:
Active Substance: thiram

Introduction: Broad-spectrum organosulfur fungicide. Traditionally used in the US for apple and wine growing. Since 2010, most fumonisins have been used in soybean production. It is avoided by animals and applied to keep fruit trees, ornamentals, etc. safe from birds, rabbits, rodents and deer. Fumonisin has also been used to treat scabies in humans, as a sunscreen and as an antiseptic applied directly to the skin or incorporated into soap. Powdered mixtures containing benomyl at or above 7%, carbofuran at or above 10%, and thiram at or above 15% are controlled under the Rotterdam Convention.

Mode of action: Multi-site touch activity (FRAC 2022). Non-specific, multi-site of action, which e.g. binds to coenzyme A, thereby inhibiting the activity of a wide range of fungal enzymes, spore germination and mycelial growth.

The way of action: protective

Resistance: International Fungicide Resistance Action Committee FRAC M 03, Group of Dithiocarbamates and their Derivatives (Electrophilic Reagents). Pathogenic bacteria are usually considered to have a low risk of resistance and do not exhibit resistance.

Introduction: Metal phosphide insecticide. Broad-spectrum fumigation insecticide, rodenticide, mainly used for fumigation of goods storage pests, grain and seed storage pests, outdoor rodents. Under dry conditions, it is safer for humans and animals, and plays a role in releasing phosphine gas by decomposing on its own after absorbing moisture, which is highly toxic to human beings. The potential danger of phosphide-based pesticides is relatively high. Therefore, in recent years, in order to reduce public exposure to phosphine-based fumigants, countries have strengthened the management of phosphine-based pesticides.

Mode of action: Mitochondrial complex IV electron transport inhibitor

The way of action: phosphine fumigation

evidence.content:
Active Substance: cyprodinil

The way of action: systemic

evidence.label: D1
evidence.name: glyphosate
evidence.content:
Active Substance: glyphosate

Introduction: Glyphosate is registered in more than 130 countries and is one of the most produced, used and sold herbicides in the world. Described by some as an "almost ideal" herbicide and a once-in-a-century discovery, glyphosate is as important to reliable global food production as penicillin is to the treatment of human disease. However, in March 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), a division of the World Health Organization, classified glyphosate as "probably carcinogenic to humans" (Group 2A) based on the results of epidemiological, animal and in vitro studies. Sites of carcinogenicity in humans: limited evidence for leukemia and/or lymphoma. Show more (Introduction to Glyphosate)

Mode of action: Inhibitor of 5-enolpyruvyl mangiferyl-3-phosphate synthase (EPSPS).

The way of action: Inactivation, endocytosis conduction

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 9. Glyphosate-resistant weeds had not yet been identified when the first genetically modified crops such as corn, oilseed rape, soybeans, and cotton were introduced in the 1990s. By 2014, glyphosate-resistant weeds dominated herbicide resistance research, with 23 resistant weeds, often referred to as "superweeds," identified in 18 countries. The most common resistant weeds are oxalis, matang, multiflora ryegrass, hard ryegrass, small whitebrier, balsam fescue, ragweed, groundsel, morningglory, tumbleweed, orang-utan, false sorghum, firleaf algae, fleabane and Palmer amaranth.

evidence.label: D2
evidence.name: paraquat dichloride
evidence.content:
Active Substance: paraquat dichloride

Introduction: It is the last step of paraquat production in the aminocyanine method, and is the most important paraquatium salt compound used in agricultural production. After glyphosate, it is the second largest herbicide in the world. It has the characteristics of quick-acting, touching, non-selective, low cost and low resistance of weeds, and is widely used in non-cultivated land, no-tillage land, and inter-row weed control of row crops. It has strong destructive effect on the green tissue of both monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants, no endosorption conduction effect, and can only whiten the drugged part. It can't destroy the roots of weeds and the seeds hidden in the soil, and there is regeneration of weeds after applying the medicine. It has poor preventive effect on plantain, polygonum, pellitory, thatching grass, duckweed and fragrant plantain. Loses activity after contact with soil.

Mode of action: Photosynthetic system Ⅰ Inhibitor. Peroxides produced during photosynthesis that damage cell membranes and cytoplasm. Specifically, bipyridine cation is rapidly absorbed by plant leaves, and then reduced to bipyridine free radicals through photosynthesis and respiration in green tissues, and then hydrogen peroxide and peroxide free radicals are formed from water and oxygen in leaf tissues by autoxidation, which are extremely destructive to the chloroplast layer membrane, so that photosynthesis and chlorophyll synthesis are stopped, and the leaves start to suffer from discoloration in 2-3 h after being drugged.

The way of action: Extinguishability, touch kills

Resistance: Resistant weeds have emerged in Western Australia. Alternating or rotating with glyphosate can delay the development of weed resistance.

evidence.label: D4
evidence.name: diquat
evidence.content:
Active Substance: diquat

Introduction: ISO 1750-1981 defines diquat as 1,1'-ethylidene-2,2'-bipyridinium and requires that the anion contained in the commercial formulation be indicated. There are two main commercial salts on the market, diquat dibromide and diquat dichloride, with diquat dibromide being the most widely used. Its dibromide is widely used. In recent years, its dichloride has also been registered in China. Regardless of the salts, the active ingredient content is expressed in terms of diquat. Diquat and Diquat dibromide or dichloride are different compounds. The spectrum and efficacy of Diquat are not as good as Paraquat, and if the problem of emergency treatment of serious human poisoning brought about by its sale and use is not solved, it will sooner or later, like Paraquat, be hard to escape the fate of being banned.

Mode of action: Photosystem I electron transport inhibitor

The way of action: Extinguishability, touch kills

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 22

evidence.label: D5
evidence.name: paraquat
evidence.content:
Active Substance: paraquat

Introduction: Paraquat is defined in ISO 1750-1981 as 1,1'-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridinium, while the anion contained is required to be indicated in commercial formulations. There are 2 face-to-face commercial salts, paraquat dichloride and paraquat bisulfate methyl ester, with its dichloride being widely used. Regardless of the salt, the active ingredient content is indicated by paraquat. Paraquat and paraquat dichloride are two compounds. Queries revealed that its toxicity and treatment accounted for the vast majority of the literature, indicating a great threat to the safety of human life. Despite all the efforts of pesticide producers (development of solid dosage forms; addition of the emetic triazolopyrimidinone to aqueous dosage forms, blue or green coloring agents, odorants and thickeners), they have not escaped the fate of being banned.

Mode of action: Photosystem I electron transport inhibitor

The way of action: Extinguishability, touch kills

Resistance: International Herbicide Resistance Action Committee/Weed Science Society of America HRAC/WSSA Group 22. Resistant weeds have emerged in Western Australia. Alternating or rotating with glyphosate may delay the development of weed resistance.
